items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: I learned more from him about music, and what music can do for people

ctx.x: Now you're talking about New Orleans.

Yeah, that's right. I always tell people like Bunk Johnson, I studied with some other very great musicians, I will say Arnold Schoenberg, whom some people consider as at least one of the two or three greatest modern composers, and other, not to knock any of the classical musicians, but as I always say, Bunk had more music in him, and I learned more from him about music, and what music can do for people, and what its real place is in life, and I ever did before.
You mean he expressed this in his own personality as well as in his music?

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: So I did record Bunk playing informally with Bertha Gonsolin, a pianist.

ctx.x: The reason I got into the business at all was partly due to these first records I mentioned, the Jazzmen, that were so badly recorded on the little machine. About a $200 list price machine it was, a federal recorder. Some kid that worked, he was a teenage kid, I guess, that worked for Grunewald's. Happened to have it. He's the only one we could find that had any blanks around that would be able to record the band in 1942 when Dave issued the records. And those records were so bad that I'll tell you one story that…

He hadn't thrown them out fortunately, but he probably would have very soon if Dave hadn't gotten back. He could have thrown them in a wastebasket. So he thought it was just a joke, you know, that he sent something to amuse him. So Dave said, no, that's the real thing. It had to be worked on and issued. So anyway, I decided after that that I couldn't do much worse. So I got a machine. My machine only cost about $40. My brother put a little secondhand machine together and then bought an amplifier. My brother was a…
This is the fourth, okay, I got the fourth reel on.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: I told Jean I'd try to get the recording date done then, if possible. So I began writing a letter to Bunk, asking if he, uh, could come over.

ctx.x: The, uh, same studio. I'd have to look that up. I looked all that up for Ralph Gleason about, uh, two or three months ago. Ralph had had the idea it was WWL. It wasn't that. Uh, that, uh, that Bunk had made his records for Jean Williams. Jean did make some records at a studio, WSMB, I guess. His—I know, WSMB, in the Maison Blanc's building in 1942. Uh, Woody, uh, I'm not real sure. I don't have the dope at hand right now. It might have been W—WL, which is the Roosevelt Hotel, possibly, at that time. But, uh,…
Well, he probably hadn't lived here since 1918, I guess.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: when Bunk came here in 1942, we went down to see Fats Pichon, Walter Pichon, who's probably a very nice guy, and I was prejudiced against him because when Bunk went and asked him to record with him, he refused.

ctx.x: I'd like to know what your personal opinion of his personality was.

I'm like, I believe, with all the musicians, and most of the better ones, you'll hear some awful reports occasionally, some musicians will say, oh, he was terrible. For instance, when we went to try to get, when Bunk came here in 1942, we went down to see Fats Pichon, Walter Pichon, who's probably a very nice guy, and I was prejudiced against him because when Bunk went and asked him to record with him, he refused. I guess it was going to be a non-union date. The union, of course, meant nothing to Bunk and all. I…
He received you very ambly, though.
